Halfway between the United States and Japan is Alaska’s Adak Island. It is one of the remote Aleutian islands.

It is a place known for its natural beauty. The coast is home to rich wildlife. Purple lupine flowers can be seen along roads through grassy hills. Hot springs cover the landscape. Snow-topped mountains and the Great Sitkin volcano rise in the distance.

It is also a strange place, with an important military history. Adak became a U.S. Army airbase during World War II to protect against a feared Japanese invasion of Alaska. Because of its closeness to Russia, it remained an important military base throughout the Cold War.

It is not easy to get to. It requires a four-hour plane trip from Anchorage. People visit Adak to hunt, watch birds, climb mountains, or examine one of the many abandoned military bases.

American writer Nicole Evatt recently described her travels there. She describes two Adaks: one filled with beautiful nature and one filled with Cold War military remains.

The old navigation station is covered with graffiti and is falling apart. The doors and windows are broken. Evatt calls the inside of the buildings “spooky.” As she walked through dark, partly wet rooms, paint was coming off the surfaces and broken equipment sat in disrepair. Through broken windows, she saw the blue-black Bering Sea crashing into nearby Horseshoe Bay.

In town, fewer than 100 people live full-time in old military houses. These houses sit in mostly empty neighbourhoods with other buildings in need of repair. So why do people stay? Some love the quiet. Others say they feel safe. Some get extra pay for remote work. People who live there often do many different jobs.

Adak locals learn to live with very limited supplies. The only food store is in the old daycare center, and it is open just a few hours on some evenings. The old high school and middle school now hold city hall, a healthcare center and the post office.

Food choices are limited. Restaurants and stores are often closed. One eatery does not open often, but when it does, it serves a large pizza for $28. Evatt wrote that it was surprisingly tasty considering how far the tomato sauce and cheese had to travel.

Source: ‘Visiting Alaska’s Distant Aleutian Islands’, VOA Learning English (learningenglish.voanews.com). Adapted by Anna Matteo from reporting by Nicole Evatt for the Associated Press. Harry Qiu began learning English as a young boy in Shanghai, China. He later came to the United States for college, where he is now learning two more languages.

Through his school, he talks one-on-one with native speakers online. When he meets his Japanese partner, Qiu helps his partner practise English. His partner helps him practise Japanese. We call this a language exchange.

Such exchanges can be one of the best ways to improve your conversation skills. Today, many websites and apps connect language learners around the world. But doing an exchange without knowing what to expect can lead to wasted time. So here are five tips.

First, ask yourself some questions. Todd Bryant runs a language exchange website with more than 35,000 users. He says the most important question is why you want to learn the language. People who have a serious reason are usually more dependable partners. Also think about how much free time you really have, and whether you want speaking practice or written messages.

Second, find the right partner. Many websites have hundreds to choose from. Bryant says to look for people who have been active on the site and have a clear reason to learn the language. It is also better to find at least two partners, because one person may not be free every week.

Third, state your expectations. Be clear in your first message about how long you would like meetings to be and how often you would like to meet. Bryant says this gives the partnership a better chance of working. But avoid being too rigid — offer more than one possible time.

Fourth, come prepared. Before each meeting, prepare some questions on a topic of your choice. This gives you the chance to look up related words, and it stops you running out of things to say ten minutes in.

Fifth, focus on communication. The main goal is conversation practice, so let your partner speak freely, even if they make mistakes. Bryant recommends giving only one or two corrections after each piece of dialogue. Qiu corrects a partner only if the person cannot finish a sentence.

Qiu’s advice to anyone who wants to try a language exchange is simple: don’t be afraid to make mistakes.

Source: ‘Five Tips for Great Language Exchanges’ by Alice Bryant, VOA Learning English (learningenglish.voanews.com). One of the best things about travelling to a new country is learning about new traditions and customs. They can be very different from our own.

When visiting a foreign country, it is smart to follow the local social rules and customs of the people who live there. This can make your stay easier and more enjoyable.

There is an expression for this that goes all the way back to ancient Rome: When in Rome, do as the Romans do.

It means that when we visit a place, we should follow the customs of that place. It shows an attitude: you are willing to change your way of doing things to fit in with those around you.

The place does not have to be a new country. It can simply be a new situation. For example, you may usually speak very loudly. But in an art museum or a library, you whisper. You follow the rules of that place.

The expression has another meaning too. When you are in an unfamiliar situation, you should follow the lead of those who know the rules. These people know how to behave with others, and how to work within the system. They blend in.

But what does Rome have to do with following other people’s customs? Here is how the story goes. More than 1500 years ago, a Christian leader, Saint Augustine, moved from Rome to Milan. In the new city, he found some parts of religious life to be different. In Rome he fasted, or did not eat, on Saturday. But in Milan, people did not fast on Saturday.

Another church leader, Saint Ambrose, gave him some advice. He said that when he goes to Rome he fasts on Saturdays, but when he is in Milan, he does not. Problem solved.

This advice has survived over the years. Some word experts say it first appeared in English around 500 years ago. We still use it today, either to give advice or to describe a situation where we have to change our behaviour to fit in.

{"fromDefaults":true,"items":{"fol":{"general":"There is no model answer: each trainee writes about their own group. It is usually the first assignment, written with little reading behind it.
• Pass a trainee who has looked carefully at their learners and reasoned honestly, even if the terminology is shaky.
• Keep Not met for missing observation or missing reasoning.
• Hold firm on specificity: a vague problem cannot be met by a targeted task. Be generous about polish.

Before you mark
• Each problem in B and C has two real examples: a named student, what they said or wrote, and the lesson stage.
• One task per problem. If several are attached for the tutor to choose from, that section is not met: choosing is the skill being assessed.
• At least one task is from a published source, and each says where it came from.
• D and E each end with one source or support the learners could use on their own: a book, a site or app, or a person. The 2.1 design includes "sources for language and/or skills development and, where appropriate, personal support systems" (syllabus p. 17).","crit":["Met: The group description says how the learners' backgrounds, previous learning and preferences shape what works with them, and D and E use those preferences.

Shortfalls:
• a list of facts with no interpretation
• preferences that D and E never refer to","Met: The grammar and pronunciation problems are real and specific, each with two named examples.

Shortfalls:
• an area that is too broad ('problems with tenses')
• examples with no student attached","Met:
• Grammar areas are named correctly
• pronunciation is described in IPA, not respelling
• terms like 'fossilised' and 'L1 interference' are used accurately

Shortfalls:
• no IPA: that fails this criterion
• a wrong symbol is only a note, unless it shows the contrast was misidentified
• occasional imprecision is tolerable; consistent misuse is not","Met:
• One task per problem, at the right level, aimed at the specific error
• at least one from a published source
• the pronunciation task has learners producing the sound

Shortfalls:
• a task on the whole area (the most common reason for resubmission)
• more than one task attached","Met: Explains why this task suits these learners and this error, and refers back to Part A.

Shortfalls: a rationale that would fit any class and any task.","Met: At least one published source used in the body of the assignment, in prose that is organised and readable.

Shortfalls: language errors matter only where they obscure the meaning."],"sections":"A · Your TP group
Met: the practical facts (size, ages, level, L1s, jobs, education); why they learn English, with a term or two from the reading (instrumental, integrative, intrinsic, extrinsic); previous learning described in a way that explains something ('grammar-translation at school, so they expect explicit rules'); learning preferences clear enough for D and E to use.
Shortfalls: facts with no interpretation; motivation asserted with no evidence; preferences missing or vague; surnames used, or students not named at all.
A is the foundation for criterion 1 and half of criterion 5. If it is thin, the rationales in D and E have nothing to refer to.

B · The grammar problem
Met: a specific area with the correct term; two examples, each with student, spoken or written, stage and correction; a real cause (L1 interference with a reference to Learner English or similar, level, fossilisation, lack of practice); the reading referenced.
Shortfalls: an area too broad ('articles', 'prepositions', 'tenses'); examples with no student, context or correction; two different errors presented as one problem; a cause that only restates the error.

C · The pronunciation problem
Met: the feature named with IPA (a sound contrast, a stress pattern, a connected-speech feature); two examples with student and both the wrong and correct forms transcribed; cause explained, usually from the L1 sound system.
Shortfalls: no IPA or IPA used wrongly; 'problems with vowels' not narrowed to a contrast; only the correct form transcribed; 'their accent' as the cause.

D · The grammar task
Met: one task, source stated, right level, aimed at the error in B; rationale refers to A and to the context in B; procedure covers set-up, what students do, timing, interaction, monitoring and feedback.
Shortfalls: a task on the general area; more than one task; a rationale that never mentions A; no monitoring or feedback.
Adapting a published task is fine and often shows more thought. The trainee should say what they changed and why.
The last bullet: one source or support for working on this on their own, named, with a reason it suits them. 'Use the internet' is not a source.

E · The pronunciation task
Met: one task, source stated, learners producing the target sound or feature (minimal-pair games, dictation to a partner, recorded self-correction); rationale refers to A and the contrast in C; full procedure as in D.
Shortfalls: discrimination only with no production; 'drill the words' or 'repeat after me' as the task; a different sound, or all vowels; no audio or model source where one is needed.
Drilling can be part of the procedure, but something else has to be the activity.
The last bullet: one source or support for this sound, as in D.","source":"From the C/18 marking guides (Oct 2026)","critText":["Showing awareness of how a learner’s/learners’ background(s), previous learning experience and learning preferences affect learning","Identifying the learner’s/learners’ language and/or skills needs","Correctly using terminology relating to the description of language systems and/or language skills","Selecting appropriate material and/or resources to aid the learner’s/learners’ language and/or skills development","Providing a rationale for using specific activities with a learner/learners","Finding, selecting and referencing information from one or more sources using written language that is clear, accurate and appropriate to the task"]},"lrt":{"general":"This one has right and wrong answers, but most analyses can be written more than one way.
• Mark accuracy and detail, not wording.
• An analysis that would mislead learners has not met criterion 1.
• One that is correct, sourced and complete passes, even if thin in places.

Before you mark
• Four items: one grammar, one functional exponent, two vocabulary.
• Each analysis covers the item in bold, not the whole sentence.
• Form, meaning, pronunciation and use are all there for each item. The 2.2 design includes all four (syllabus p. 17).
• A real reference is named for each item. 'Google' or an unnamed website is not an appropriate source for criterion 3.
• The items are not the basis of an assessed TP lesson. Cambridge: materials for this task "should not be used as the basis for assessed TP lessons, or vice versa" (Handbook 9.2.1).","crit":["Met:
• The meaning fits this letter
• the form is broken down accurately
• the pronunciation is correctly transcribed and stressed

Shortfalls:
• errors of fact (wrong tense, wrong stress, a meaning that does not fit)
• CCQs that use the item itself
• inaccurate phonemic script (missing stress alone is usually a note)","Met: Terms are accurate and specific: 'present perfect simple' not 'past tense'; 'weak form' and 'contraction' used correctly; word stress kept apart from sentence stress.

Shortfalls: consistent misuse. Occasional imprecision is tolerable.","Met: At least one named published source for each item (a grammar reference, a learner dictionary, a pronunciation source), with page numbers where the source has them.

Shortfalls:
• 'Google', an unnamed website, or AI alone
• a bibliography with nothing cited against the items","Met: Organised and readable, using the table properly.

Shortfalls: language errors matter only where they obscure the analysis or suggest the trainee has misunderstood the point."],"sections":"Meaning and clarification
Met: the meaning in this context only; CCQs that genuinely test the meaning, each with an expected answer, usually three or four; timelines, clines or personal examples where they help.
Shortfalls: a dictionary definition copied out; CCQs that use the item itself ('Is she staying?' to check 's staying); CCQs with no answers; CCQs that check the letter, not the language.

Form
Met: the item broken into parts a learner could copy from the board; parts named, with a formula where it helps; what changes and what is fixed (contractions, endings, word order); for lexis, part of speech, dependent prepositions, countability, spelling changes.
Shortfalls: naming the structure without breaking it down; a formula that would not generate the sentence; phrasal verbs with no word on separability.

Pronunciation
Met: correct phonemic script; word stress and sentence stress marked; weak forms, contractions and linking identified; likely problem sounds named.
Shortfalls: invented notation ('de-LIGHT-ed'); no stress marked; the weak form or contraction missed, when it is usually the point of the item.

Use and appropriacy
Met: when and with whom, how formal; any restriction (spoken or written, what it is not used for); 'neutral' said where it is neutral.
Shortfalls: row left blank or 'N/A'; register asserted with no basis.

Anticipated problems and solutions
Met: meaning, form AND pronunciation all covered; problems specific to these learners; a realistic classroom solution for each, linked to the techniques above.
Shortfalls: only one or two of the three (pronunciation is the usual omission); problems with no solution; 'students may find this difficult' with nothing behind it.

Model · He's staying for two weeks (grammar)
Meaning: a fixed future arrangement, already made; not a prediction or a decision made now. CCQs: Is this happening now, or later? (Later.) Has he decided already? (Yes.) Is it arranged, or is he thinking about it? (Arranged.) Timeline: 'now', then a block at Easter labelled 'arranged'.
Form: subject + be + verb-ing. He is staying, He's staying. Time expression follows: for two weeks.
Pronunciation: /hiːz ˈsteɪɪŋ/. is contracts to /z/; stress on STAY-.
Use: neutral, very common in speech for arrangements; odd for something not agreed (going to, might).
Problems: meaning read as 'happening now' (timeline, contrast with 'He's staying with me tonight'); be omitted, *He staying (build the form, drill the contraction); contraction dropped (model and drill /hiːz/).
References: Swan, Practical English Usage (2016), pp. 65–66; Parrott, Grammar for English Language Teachers (2010), p. 172.

Model · settle in (vocabulary)
Meaning: to become comfortable in a new place or situation over time. Here, getting used to living in Lisbon. CCQs: Is this quick or does it take time? (It takes time.) Is the writer comfortable now? (Yes, more than at first.) Can you settle in on your first day? (Not really.) Where else could you settle in? (A new job, a new school.)
Form: phrasal verb, intransitive. She settled in, not *she settled in the flat (settle into the flat). Regular past: settled /d/.
Pronunciation: /ˌsetəl ˈɪn/. Main stress on the particle, in; secondary stress on SET-. Schwa in the second syllable of settle; the /l/ links into in.
Use: neutral to informal, very common in speech; about people, not objects; often with adverbs (settle in quickly, settle in well).
Problems: confused with settle down (contrast in examples, check with CCQs); treated as transitive, *I settled in the new city (show the pattern, give settle into); stress put on settle so in is lost (mark stress on the board, model the linked form and drill).
References: Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary, 'settle in'; Thornbury, How to Teach Vocabulary (2002), p. 7.","source":"From the C/18 marking guides (Oct 2026)","critText":["Analysing language correctly for teaching purposes","Correctly using terminology relating to form, meaning and phonology when analysing language","Accessing reference materials and referencing information they have learned about language to an appropriate source","Using written language that is clear, accurate and appropriate to the task"]},"lsrt":{"general":"There is no answer key: trainees choose their own text, subskills and tasks, so many answers can pass.
• Pass a trainee who has understood the principle and applied it reasonably, even if a task could be sharper.
• Right thinking said awkwardly is a pass. Fluent writing that misunderstands what a subskill is, is not.
• Where you are undecided, talk to the second marker before recording Not met.

Before you mark
• Answer keys are attached for the tasks.
• The tasks are reading tasks on the text and a productive task that grows from it. Lead-ins and pre-teaching are outside the brief.
• The text and tasks are not the basis of an assessed TP lesson. Cambridge: they "should not be used as the basis for assessed TP lessons, or vice versa" (Handbook 9.2.1).","crit":["Met: 'Gist', 'specific information', 'detail', 'receptive', 'productive' and 'subskill' are used accurately.

Shortfalls: consistent confusion, such as calling a detail task 'gist'. Occasional slips are tolerable.","Met:
• The first task develops reading for gist
• the second develops specific information or detail
• a productive skill is identified for the follow-up
• all fit the text and this class

Shortfalls: skills named with no link to the text or the class.","Met:
• The tasks are attached and usable in class
• each comes with an answer key
• the rationale ties each task to the subskill it develops and to these learners

Shortfalls: a rationale that only describes the task again in other words.","Met: At least one real, correctly attributed source used in the body to support a point about skills or subskills.

Shortfalls: a source in the bibliography that is never used."],"sections":"A · Choosing the text
Met: says which text; justifies it against level, length, interests, genre and whether it supports two reading tasks and a productive task; refers to this class (mid-20s, mixed nationality, career and travel, two taking IELTS); some awareness of why it is manageable at B1.
Shortfalls: topic interest only; generic statements that fit any of the three texts; no reference to this class; a text chosen and then tasks that do not suit it.
All three texts are defensible. Mark the reasoning, not the choice.

B · First reading task
Met: a gist task; what reading for gist is, from the reading; how the task develops it, linked to reading outside class; a procedure with set-up, what students do, interaction, timing and feedback; a realistic task with an answer key that needs the text.
Shortfalls: never explaining what gist is; a 'gist' task that needs detailed reading, or can be answered from the headings; feedback missing from the procedure (the most common gap); no answer key; reading in the bibliography but not used here; a lead-in or pre-teaching stage.
A gist task with a slightly generous time limit still passes. One that needs every line read does not.

C · Second reading task
Met: names the subskill (specific information or detail) and explains it from the reading; how the task develops it; full procedure; a task with an answer key that depends on the text.
